headline: At depth one there is no chain to collapse, so the case prices each library's floor cost per element: next-yak compiles to a bare tagged element and leads, while the runtime lanes already give up 2 to 4× before any wrapping begins.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

microbench.why: One styled button and no chain, so what separates the lanes is the cost of getting a class onto a single element. `next-yak` compiles to `jsx("button", { className: "yMtpbN9" })` with no component left at all and renders at 2.27M renders/s, above hand-written `vanilla` at 1.96M, which still calls a function per instance. `next-yak-nofold` at 1.47M is the same source with folding switched off and prices the `Yak` wrapper at 1.54× on its own. `emotion` at 495,000 and `panda-props` at 693,000 do their per-instance work regardless of depth, which is why this control matters: much of their compose-3 and compose-6 cost is this figure repeated.

autocannon.why: `next-yak` serves 1,796 req/s against 1,607 for `vanilla` and 1,256 for `next-yak-nofold`. The gap between the two yak lanes is the wrapper call and nothing else, since their source is identical and only `foldStatic` differs.

attribution.why: `next-yak` totals 0.569 ms with 0.227 ms of lib self-time and nothing charged to a component, because folding removed the only one. `vanilla` totals 0.651 ms and books 0.217 ms as component self-time instead. Past those two the ordering follows how much each library computes per element: `styled-components` 1.24 ms, `panda` 1.35 ms with the work in the component slice, `emotion` 2.17 ms.

hydrate.why: Twelve lanes hydrate between 43.7 ms and 66.9 ms with no clear relation to their render ranking, and `stylex` at 85.4 ms sits far above its own sibling lane at 44.9 ms, which reads as spread rather than mechanism. The separation that does reproduce is `goober` and `styled-components` at 134 ms, both building their sheet in the client before React attaches.

inp.why: All fifteen lanes answer one click between 7.1 ms and 8.6 ms. A single unwrapped button leaves an interaction nothing to re-derive, so this axis is flat by construction.

mount.why: Eight lanes mount between 66.3 ms and 71.6 ms, `next-yak` first at 66.3 ms, because parse and layout dominate and every lane produces the same DOM. The sheet-building lanes trail from 90.4 ms to 103 ms.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane, costing 0.130 ms to 0.206 ms. A single element with a settled sheet gives the engine identical work everywhere.

payload.why: `vanilla` sets the floor at 2,700 gz B with no JS. `next-yak-css` adds 346 B of library and `next-yak` 1,152 B for the wrapper runtime. The runtime lanes are dominated by themselves: 13.0 kB of JS for `emotion` and 13.5 kB for `styled-components`, five times the entire `vanilla` page for the same one button.

nsweep.why: `next-yak` holds 1.64 ms at the largest size against 2.66 ms for its no-fold lane, so the wrapper's cost scales with the count rather than amortizing away. `emotion` at 8.64 ms shows what per-instance serialization does to a slope.

crossCase: Read with the Examples `compose-3` and `compose-6` shown below, which wrap this same button two and five more times. `next-yak` runs the three depths at 2.27M, 1.45M and 1.49M renders/s: the drop from one to three buys back a `__yak_button` component that depth one does not need, and depth six is free because six levels concatenate into that same single component. `vanilla` pays once per level instead, 1.96M to 1.33M to 919,000.
